Bell or Horn

At Staniforth Road in Sheffield, a tramway crosses a footpath at an intersection of two busy roads. There are no pedestrian light signals at the crossing to indicate whether it is safe or unsafe to step onto it, and the design includes no physical barrier. Someone approaching from the south walks beside a 45-metre fence. The first 40 metres of it are built primarily to stop road vehicles running onto the tramway, and the differing gradient profiles on either side leave a drop in height between the pavement and the track. Only the final five metres are there to separate pedestrians from the tramway, and that section follows the pavement downwards towards the crossing. At the end of it a signal post carries a blue sign reading TRAMWAY LOOK BOTH WAYS. Turning east to cross, a person can see two more of the same sign, one on either side. The words are painted on the pavement as well, immediately before a short stretch of tactile paving, in a reminder of rule 33 of the Highway Code. Past the tactile paving the surface becomes paved brick, with segregated ballasted track to the south and raised granite cobbles to the north. The pavement is also part of a National Cycle Route, and signage and line markings mark off where cyclists belong.

The report sets out what all of this rests on. "Safe use of the crossing," it states, "is reliant on pedestrians correctly responding to the signage and markings, and observing or hearing approaching trams."

Approximately 30 metres before the crossing there is an audible warning board. It faces the driver rather than the pedestrian, and it reminds them of a requirement to sound an audible warning on the approach to the footpath and vehicle crossings. It was originally fitted in response to an accident involving a pedestrian at this same crossing in 2005.

What it asks for is set out in the operator's rules and operational standards, which require drivers to "give a compulsory appropriate audible warning of the approach of the tram," and add that "all warnings must be of adequate length to ensure third parties are able to react and move clear of the tram approach." A tram carries two devices for this. The standards specify the horn at one location only, Sheffield Road bridge, which is not near Staniforth Road; "at all other audible warning boards, it is the driver's decision whether to sound the bell or the horn." The training document drivers learn from, MEI-CAT Phase Two, requires an "appropriate audible warning of the approach of the tram", with warnings of "adequate length" — the same two words again.

RAIB finds that "the absence of specific details on audible warnings within operational rules and training documents creates the potential for inconsistency between drivers on the type and length of warnings which are sounded at audible warning boards across the network." After the accident its inspectors stood at the outbound board and watched what passing trams did. They used either their bell or their horn, "with drivers generally opting for louder and longer warnings during darkness."

Both devices on the tram involved were tested afterwards against Railway Group Standard GMRT 2484 issue 2 and the tramway standard LRSSB-LRG 5.0. They met the requirements, were fully operational, sounded clearly, and were accurately recorded on the on-tram data recorder, "which records bell and horn activation on the same channel."

The driver had booked on at 09:46 on Sunday 22 June 2025. They worked three days a week and this was their first shift after two rest days. At 15:46 tram 101 left Middlewood, outbound towards Meadowhall Interchange, lightly loaded with around 30 passengers.

Two young people, aged 15 and 17, had been racing at Woodbourn Road athletics stadium and were running a cool-down circuit around the grounds. They were not residents of Sheffield. They came a few times each summer for race meets, and were not familiar with the area, or with tram networks generally. The circuit is 1.2 km, takes about six minutes, and crosses the tramway twice. They had completed it fewer than ten times, and had never encountered a tram while crossing.

No requests were made for the Woodbourn Road stop, so the tram passed through without stopping. Shortly afterwards the driver saw the two of them on the pavement, running ahead of the tram and alongside the track. The driver accelerated to line speed, using the service brake on the descending gradient to stay at or below the 30 mph limit, and made a short hazard brake application approximately 30 metres from the start of the crossing to bring the tram down for the 15 mph reduction. The signal for the junction showed a proceed aspect from the moment it came into view. Around one second before they were struck, the two runners turned to their right and ran across the tramway and directly into the path of the tram. They did not look towards it before stepping onto the crossing. Less than a second before the collision the driver applied the hazard brake and sounded the horn at the same time. The tram was travelling at approximately 17 mph.

One of them was pushed clear by the other and sustained minor injuries. The other fell with the lower half of their body underneath the front of the tram and was carried forward by equipment beneath it for about six metres. The tram stopped roughly four seconds after the hazard brake was applied, about 12 metres beyond the point of collision. The area past the crossing included the raised cobbles, which possibly exacerbated one pedestrian's injuries. Both were taken to hospital, one seriously injured. Nobody on board was hurt. The driver was tested for drugs and alcohol and the results were negative.

Then the recorders. "The pedestrians did not hear a warning from the tram before the crossing," the report states. Footage from inside the cab shows the driver had their hand on the control that sounds the bell or the horn. The driver stated that they sounded the bell; the movements required are only slight, and the footage cannot resolve whether they did. The recorder logged no bell at the audible warning board, and so, RAIB concludes, "it is therefore probably the case that the tram driver did not sound an audible warning as required." The horn it did log, "within a second of the pedestrians turning right into the path of the tram but less than a second before the collision, when the pedestrians were already on the crossing, and with insufficient time to act as an effective warning."

In September 2008, on London Tramlink, a tram collided with a cyclist at the Morden Hall Park footpath crossing and the cyclist later died. The driver had sounded the audible warnings. The cyclist may have been wearing headphones, which would have prevented them hearing, and the approach did not encourage cyclists to look towards eastbound trams. In September 2018, near Saughton tram stop in Edinburgh, a pedestrian was struck and fatally injured, and there the bell had been rung repeatedly on the approach: "the audible warning was not sufficiently loud for it to be heard and acted upon by the pedestrian until it was too late."

The report gathers the others too. In October 2005 a tram struck and seriously injured a pedestrian at Staniforth Road itself, after they stepped onto the crossing directly in front of it; the investigation then found that the driver's ability to assess the risk may have been negatively affected by the fence on the approach. In May 2012 a pedestrian near Sandilands tram stop in Croydon was struck and seriously injured, having not looked, at a crossing where trams on the nearest track came from behind. In December 2016, at Woodbourn Road tram stop — where the two runners had themselves crossed the tramway earlier that afternoon — a pedestrian who had just got off an inbound tram was struck and fatally injured by a non-stop outbound tram at around 13 mph. They were seemingly unaware it was approaching, "and the tram did not give an audible warning to indicate that it was passing non-stop through the tram stop."

The remedies form their own line. After 2005 at Staniforth Road, the audible warning board was installed and a 24-metre section of fence was redesigned. After the death at Woodbourn Road in 2016, RAIB recommended that the operator review its operational standards against its training material, with the stated intent "that all tram drivers drive to the same set of requirements, irrespective of when they were initially trained." Nine years later, RAIB records that more effective implementation of that recommendation "could have addressed the inconsistencies in audible warnings for users of the footpath crossing which were a factor in this accident."

Observing and hearing are joined by an "or", as though either would do. But looking is a property of the crossing. The sightline is there whenever anyone is, and it does not have to be sent. Hearing, at Staniforth Road, is a message with a sender: someone reaching for a control, choosing between two devices, deciding what length is adequate. Its ordinary state is silence. And on every previous circuit those two runners had made — fewer than ten of them, none with a tram on the track — the silence had been true. A channel that is almost always silent, and almost always silent truthfully, teaches the people who use it that silence is information.
